clinicalPearls: A large branching stone that fills the renal pelvis and extends into two or more calyces, taking the shape of a stag's horn
Most are struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate and carbonate apatite) related to chronic infection with urease-producing organisms, though a minority are cystine or uric acid
They may be surprisingly asymptomatic or present with vague loin ache, recurrent urinary infection or haematuria rather than classic colic
Complications include recurrent pyelonephritis, sepsis, progressive loss of renal function and, rarely, squamous cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis
Non-contrast CT defines the stone burden and pelvicalyceal anatomy for treatment planning
Left untreated, a staghorn calculus carries a substantial risk of kidney loss and life-threatening sepsis
Treatment aims for complete stone clearance, most often by percutaneous nephrolithotomy, because residual fragments perpetuate infection and regrowth
Culture-directed antibiotics against the urease organism are an essential adjunct to surgical clearance
reference.pathophysiology: A staghorn calculus is defined by its shape and extent rather than its composition, but the great majority arise from chronic infection with urease-producing bacteria that alkalinise the urine and drive rapid precipitation of struvite and carbonate apatite within the pelvicalyceal system. Because bacteria are incorporated into the stone, infection persists and the calculus enlarges to occupy the collecting system. Continuing infection and obstruction cause inflammation, scarring and progressive parenchymal destruction; non-infective staghorns can also form from cystine or uric acid when a heavy solute load fills the collecting system.
additionalDifferentials: Struvite versus cystine versus uric acid composition of the staghorn
Medullary sponge kidney with heavy nephrocalcinosis
additionalInvestigations: Non-contrast CT to map stone extent and calyceal anatomy
Urine culture and sensitivity to identify the causative organism
Assessment of split renal function, such as nuclear renography, to weigh salvage against nephrectomy
Serum renal function and inflammatory markers
Metabolic screen for a non-infective stone nidus
redFlags: Sepsis from an infected obstructed staghorn kidney
A poorly functioning kidney harbouring chronic infection
Suspicion of squamous cell carcinoma within a chronic staghorn
reference.prognosis: Complete clearance with eradication of infection offers the best chance of preserving function and preventing recurrence; incompletely treated staghorns frequently recur, and long-standing disease can lead to a non-functioning kidney requiring nephrectomy.
pitfalls: Managing with antibiotics alone without addressing the stone
Accepting incomplete clearance, which virtually guarantees recurrence
Failing to assess residual renal function before deciding on treatment
Overlooking malignancy in a chronically infected, calcified kidney
management: Complete stone clearance is the goal; percutaneous nephrolithotomy is first-line for most staghorn calculi, sometimes combined with other modalities
Culture-directed antimicrobials perioperatively to treat the associated infection, given the struvite stones harbour urease-producing organisms
Urease inhibition with acetohydroxamic acid in selected non-surgical struvite cases to slow stone growth
Metabolic evaluation with targeted prophylaxis for non-infective cystine or uric acid stones, including urinary alkalinisation and high fluid intake
Assessment of split renal function to weigh salvage against nephrectomy of a chronically infected, non-functioning kidney
Prompt drainage (nephrostomy or ureteric stent) and resuscitation for obstruction and urosepsis
Surveillance imaging and urine cultures for recurrence and residual fragments that act as a nidus for regrowth
